hints: Start with the completed nucleus row - what does having a true nucleus tell you about the big divide between cell types?
Think about which of the listed structures need internal membranes to exist - which cell type has almost no internal membranes?
Recall which structure stores cell sap and maintains turgor - is that needed for support in plants or in animals?
Recall which structure organises the spindle in animal cell division and is missing from most plant cells.
walkthrough:
Use the nucleus row as your rule**
Both animal and plant cells are eukaryotic, so they have a true nucleus surrounded by a nuclear envelope with linear DNA. Prokaryotic cells have no nucleus, only a circular DNA loop free in the cytoplasm. That same rule applies to almost all other membrane-bound organelles.

Prokaryotes lack the endomembrane system**
Rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi body are both made of membranes. RER with ribosomes makes and folds proteins, Golgi modifies and packages them. Prokaryotes are much smaller with no internal membranes except the cell surface membrane, so they have neither. Both animal and plant eukaryotes have both.

Pick out the specialists**
A large permanent vacuole filled with cell sap gives a plant cell turgor and stores solutes. Animal cells have only small temporary vacuoles if any, and prokaryotes have none. Centrioles make the spindle and form cilia and flagella in animal cells. Most plant cells and all prokaryotic cells lack centrioles.

Final answer: large permanent vacuole: animal X, plant ✓, prokaryotic X; rough endoplasmic reticulum: animal ✓, plant ✓, prokaryotic X; Golgi body: animal ✓, plant ✓, prokaryotic X; centrioles: animal ✓, plant X, prokaryotic X.

hints: Look at P at the top edge of the cell - these are tiny finger-like folds of the cell surface membrane forming a brush border.
walkthrough:
Recognise the brush border**
P points to the regular finger-like projections on the free surface of this intestinal epithelial cell. They are folds of the cell surface membrane called microvilli. Together they form the brush border and greatly increase surface area for rapid absorption of digested food.

hints: Identify Q from its sausage shape and folded inner membrane - what process always happens in this organelle when oxygen is present?
Link that product to how glucose, amino acids and ions are taken up from the gut when their concentration is already higher inside the cell.
walkthrough:
Identify Q as a mitochondrion**
Q shows the typical mitochondrion structure with an outer membrane and a highly folded inner membrane forming cristae. Many mitochondria packed in this cell is a clue that absorption is very energy-demanding.

Link respiration to absorption**
Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, releasing ATP. Absorbed nutrients such as glucose and amino acids often have to be moved by active transport against a concentration gradient, plus some uptake by endocytosis. That ATP supply directly powers the carrier proteins and membrane activity for absorption.
Final answer: Q is a mitochondrion, site of aerobic respiration producing ATP; ATP is used for active transport of digested food molecules against a concentration gradient into the cell.
